subject: pathology
title: Sickle cell disease and thalassaemias

steps.tx: **Sickle cell disease** follows a single point mutation that replaces glutamate with valine at position six of the beta globin chain. The resulting **haemoglobin S** polymerises when deoxygenated and forms rigid fibres that deform red cells into sickle shapes. Sickled cells haemolyse early and block small vessels, which explains chronic anaemia with painful ischaemic episodes. **Fetal haemoglobin** inhibits polymerisation, so infants remain protected early and drugs that raise fetal haemoglobin improve the disease.
steps.say: A single valine substitution creates haemoglobin S that polymerises whenever oxygen levels fall inside red cells. Rigid sickled cells haemolyse early and block small vessels throughout the body during a crisis. Fetal haemoglobin blocks polymerisation effectively, so infants stay protected and treatment aims to raise its level.

rows: Microcytosis, target cells, nucleated red cells

steps.tx: The film shows elongated **sickled red cells** with pointed ends beside round **target cells** and a bluish polychromatic cell that reflects reticulocytosis. The inset of normal red cells highlights how abnormal the sickled forms appear under the microscope during a crisis. Recognising sickle cells on a film matters because it supports **sickle cell disease** and prompts urgent assessment for pain, chest symptoms and anaemia. In the exam, sickle morphology links the mutation to haemolysis and vessel blockage.
steps.say: This film shows pointed sickled cells beside target cells and a young bluish cell from increased production. The normal inset makes the abnormal shapes easier to recognise under the microscope during revision. Sickled cells matter greatly because they haemolyse early and block vessels throughout the body in a crisis.

steps.tx: Vaso occlusive crises cause severe pain, swollen fingers in toddlers called dactylitis, and **acute chest syndrome** with fever, chest pain and a new lung infiltrate. Acute chest syndrome remains the leading cause of death and needs urgent assessment in any febrile patient with chest symptoms. The spleen first traps blood during **splenic sequestration** with a rapid fall in haemoglobin, then infarcts repeatedly toward autosplenectomy with Howell Jolly bodies. Transcranial Doppler screening identifies children who need preventive transfusion to reduce stroke risk.
steps.say: Blocked vessels cause painful crises, swollen fingers in toddlers and acute chest syndrome with fever and breathlessness. The spleen traps blood dangerously in young children and then infarcts away after repeated injury over years. Doppler screening finds children at high stroke risk so preventive transfusion can protect the brain.

steps.tx: **Beta thalassaemia major** presents after six months of age as fetal haemoglobin falls and severe microcytic anaemia develops in the infant. Unbalanced alpha chains precipitate inside precursors and destroy them, so **ineffective erythropoiesis** expands the marrow and deforms growing bones. The skull shows a crew haircut appearance and the liver and spleen enlarge from extramedullary blood formation. Regular transfusion sustains growth but loads iron into the heart, liver and endocrine organs without **iron chelation** therapy.
steps.say: This disease appears as fetal haemoglobin falls and severe anaemia develops during the first year of life. Expanded marrow deforms the skull and enlarges the liver and spleen in affected children everywhere. Transfusion sustains growth and life, but iron overload damages the heart unless chelation removes the excess.

vis.caption: Beta thalassaemia major: marrow expansion, ineffective erythropoiesis, and iron overload

steps.tx: **Alpha thalassaemia** severity depends on how many of the four alpha genes are deleted in each patient. One or two deletions cause mild microcytosis with normal electrophoresis and can mimic iron deficiency or beta trait. Three deletions cause **haemoglobin H disease** with moderate haemolysis and HbH inclusions inside red cells on special staining. Four deletions cause **hydrops fetalis** with haemoglobin Bart that is usually fatal without intrauterine transfusion support.
steps.say: Alpha thalassaemia becomes more severe as more alpha genes are deleted from the normal four copies. One or two deletions cause mild microcytosis with normal electrophoresis, while three deletions cause haemoglobin H disease. Four deletions produce fatal hydrops, so gene counting predicts the phenotype precisely in examination questions.

steps.tx: Diagnosis combines the blood film with **haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC** and genetic testing when the pattern remains uncertain. Beta thalassaemia trait raises HbA2, while homozygous sickle disease shows predominant HbS without normal HbA on the tracing. Iron deficiency must be excluded before labelling a patient with thalassaemia trait because both cause microcytosis. **Newborn screening** enables early penicillin prophylaxis and vaccination that transformed childhood survival in sickle cell disease.
steps.say: Electrophoresis separates these disorders because beta trait raises one fraction while sickle disease shows predominant haemoglobin S. Iron deficiency must be excluded first since it also causes small red cells in many patients. Newborn screening allows protective penicillin and vaccines that greatly improve childhood survival in sickle disease.
